title: The history of walking in New Zealand

paragraphs.text: New Zealand is a country with a long tradition of travelling on foot. In the early days of settlement the Maori people, who lived in New Zealand before Europeans arrived, are known to have regularty walked great distances. The long sandy beaches that surround so much of the country made perfect pathways, and Maori oral history records many Joumeys made there. By the time Europeans arrived, inland parts of the country were already crossed by a network of trails. European travellers observed in their letters that the vegetation had been cut back from trails so as to provide an easy route for walkers. The first Europeans walked for a variety of reasons: John Logan Campbell set off on foot in many different parts of the country determined to expand his business interests, while the scientist William Colenso walked vast distances in order to expand contemporary knowledge of the natural world. Sir George Grey walked too. In 1849 he made a remarkable journey on foot from Auckland to Lake Taupo, in all covering nearly 300 kilometres, to attend a prominent Maori chief's funeral after the leader had been killed in a landslide.

Then as the modern nation began to take shape, the once serious nature of these early walks started to change. In the 1880s, the Milford Track was cut through the forests of New Zealand's South Island, passing through the majestic landscape of the Mackinnon Pass and beneath the drama of the Sutherland Falls. The Milford Track represents a departure, because it had no commercial or administrative goal but was built only as a way of providing recreation, and today is one of the most famous walks in the world. As larger cities began to develop in the twentieth century, the urban populations demanded shorter walks, perhaps with an overnight stay, that were within a reasonable distance of their homes. So in the 1920s, the Wellington Walking Club volunteers constructed the first huts and tracks in the nearby Tararua Ranges, specifically for the use of dity residents. Govemment interest in building tracks, however, was slight, being restricted mostly to the activitles of the Forest Service, which cut tracks in the 1950s for hunters, especially those employed to cull deer. Soon afterwards perhaps the most famous of all New Zealand walkers took to the trail: the publisher and patriot A. H. Reed. In 1960, aged 85, Reed walked the length of the country from north to south, mostly on the main highways, with people turning out in every small town to clap him through. The remarkable diary Reed kept as he travelled became an instant classic that is still widely read today, doing a great deal to cement a passion for long-distance walking in the culture of contemporary New Zealand.

But by the late 1960s, the roads had more than just an occasional car rolling along between towns. The road had now become a high-speed, dangerous place and if the walker wanted peace and quiet, or solitude, then there had to be a dedicated trail. America had opened the 3,400-kilometre Appalachian Trail in 1937. England followed in 1965 with the far shorter but generally admired Pennine Way, and this seems to have been the trail that served as a particular inspiration for New Zealanders. The idea of bullding a 'scenic trall’ the length of New Zealand was written into the handbook of the country's Walkways Commission In 1976, but it remained no more than a good intention for years. The only real advance was a change in name: the 'scenic trail’ came to be called Te Araroa – meaning ‘The Long Pathway’. Construction of Te Araroa actually started in 1999 when a citizens' group began work. Since then, progress on the project has sometimes been slow, but now that the Department of Conservation has become involved the project is nearing completion.

Thousands of walkers have already done sections of Te Araroa trail, and although the track isn't formally complete, it is possible to walk the entire distance from Cape Reinga in the north of the country to Bluff in the south, using the roads to fill in for uncompleted sections of the track. It is antidpated that the final track will take approximately frve months to walk from end to end. The New Zealand landscape on either side is a startling place, with huge forests, wild scenery, an occasional river to cross and, as walkers pass through more than 70 urban centres en route, a free and easy culture.
